hints: Focus on the two conditions together, both starting compounds must dissolve, but mixing them must make something that cannot dissolve.
Remember the classic white precipitate test for sulfate ions, barium sulfate, $\text{BaSO}_4$, is insoluble while most other chlorides, nitrates and magnesium salts are soluble.
Think about swapping the ions over, which pair gives soluble starting solutions plus one insoluble combination that drops out as a solid?
walkthrough:
**Check what L and M must be**

Both L and M are Group 2 compounds that dissolve in water. So we can immediately reject any option that contains an insoluble starting compound.

Rule to remember: Group 2 nitrates and chlorides are soluble, sulfates get less soluble down the group, carbonates are insoluble.

**Think about ion exchange on mixing**

When two salt solutions mix, the cations and anions swap partners. A precipitate forms only if one of the new combinations is insoluble.

Key precipitation reaction:
$$\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s)$$

**Apply this to the pair**

Soluble $\text{BaCl}_2$ provides $\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq)$ and soluble $\text{MgSO}_4$ provides $\text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq)$. On mixing they meet and form insoluble white $\text{BaSO}_4$.

The other product is $\text{MgCl}_2$, which is soluble, so it stays in solution:
$$\text{BaCl}_2(aq) + \text{MgSO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s) + \text{MgCl}_2(aq)$$

options.A: Both barium chloride, $\text{BaCl}_2$, and magnesium sulfate, $\text{MgSO}_4$, are soluble. On mixing, $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ combine to give insoluble white barium sulfate, $\text{BaSO}_4(s)$. This fits all three statements perfectly.
options.B: Barium sulfate, $\text{BaSO}_4$, is insoluble in water, so it could never be L or M as a solution to start with. Students who choose this remember the precipitate but forget the starting compounds must both be soluble.
options.C: Both barium nitrate, $\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2$, and magnesium chloride, $\text{MgCl}_2$, are soluble, but swapping ions gives barium chloride and magnesium nitrate, both of which are also soluble. No precipitate would form, as all nitrates and most chlorides are soluble.
options.D: Barium carbonate, $\text{BaCO}_3$, is insoluble in water, so it cannot be a starting solution. This traps students who know carbonate gives a white precipitate with acids or with magnesium ions but forget the solubility condition for L and M.
